papers.abstract: After outpatient breast surgery, opioids are routinely prescribed in far greater quantity than patients consume, leaving a preventable reservoir of leftover pills at risk for misuse and diversion. This study evaluated a preoperative educational intervention and assessed whether opioid prescribing after outpatient breast surgical oncology (BSO) operations aligns with actual consumption and patient preference. In this prospective quality improvement study, patients undergoing outpatient BSO operations (n = 227) at a single cancer center from October 2025 through May 2026 received a preoperative storage and disposal handout and completed a postoperative survey. Prescriptions followed Overdose Prevention Engagement Network guidelines. Opioids were converted to oral morphine equivalents (OMEs). The primary comparison was prescribed versus consumed OMEs, assessed overall and across five surgical groups, together with retrospective patient preference, storage, and disposal. The median OME prescribed was 50 (IQR, 30-100) compared with 5 (IQR, 0-25) consumed (P < 0.001). Prescribing increased with the extent of surgery, whereas consumption remained low across all groups. In retrospect, 62% of the patients preferred fewer opioids. Two thirds stored opioids properly, exceeding historical rates, whereas disposal was uncommon at follow-up evaluation (7%), although most of the patients intended to dispose. A gap between opioids prescribed and consumed persisted despite prescribing concordant with national guidelines, and most patients preferred fewer opioids in retrospect. A brief educational intervention was associated with favorable storage but limited early disposal. These findings support prospective protocols that individualize opioid prescribing and reinforce disposal after outpatient breast operations.

papers.abstract: Neoadjuvant chemotherapy (NACT) is increasingly used in locally advanced gallbladder cancer (LAGBC), achieving pathological complete response (pCR) in some patients. We investigated factors predicting pCR and its impact on survival. This observational cohort study assessed all consecutive patients with LAGBC undergoing curative resection after NACT, from January 2015 to December 2022. We assessed pCR incidence (absence of viable tumor cells in the sampled gallbladder and lymph node), associated factors, and survival outcomes. In total, 86 patients were included in the final analysis. The Mandard tumor regression score was evaluable in 83 patients; 11 of these patients (13.25%) experienced pCR. Although patients with pCR had the best survival, pathological responders (Mandard grades 1-2) demonstrated better overall survival (median not reached) than the 32 months for poor responders (Mandard 3-5) (p = 0.048). Responders had disease-free survival of 31 months versus 9.2 months for poor responders (p = 0.057). Neither the multiagent chemotherapy nor number of cycles correlated with pathological response. pCR was achieved in 13.25% of patients with LAGBC after NACT. Although patients with pCR fared best, graded pathological response correlated with improved overall survival and DFS. Identifying factors that predict pCR has implications for treatment strategies and warrants investigation in larger prospective studies.

papers.abstract: Ionizing radiation from medical imaging may increase brain tumor risk. To quantify brain tumor risk associated with radiation exposure from medical imaging in children and adolescents. Retrospective cohort study of children born from 1996 through 2016 who were enrolled from birth in 6 US health care systems or Ontario, Canada, and were alive and cancer-free at age 2 years, with follow-up through December 31, 2017 (US sites), and December 31, 2024 (Ontario). Cumulative radiation dose to the brain from medical imaging, lagged by 2 years. Incident brain or other central nervous system tumors. Hazard ratios (HRs) were estimated using Cox proportional hazards models for categorical dose, and excess relative risks (ERRs) were estimated using linear dose-response models for continuous dose. Among 3 704 860 children (1 900 285 [51.3%] male) followed up for 45 671 641 person-years (mean follow-up, 12.3 years), 1536 brain tumors were diagnosed. Mean radiation dose from 1 head computed tomography (CT) examination was 66.2 mGy (SD, 22.2). Among children with cumulative dose of 1 mGy or greater, mean cumulative dose was 73 mGy (SD, 95) overall and 100 mGy (SD, 105) among those diagnosed with brain tumors. Compared with no exposure, brain tumor risk increased with cumulative dose (>0 to <1 mGy: HR, 1.12 [95% CI, 1.01-1.26]; 1 to <5 mGy: HR, 1.71 [95% CI, 0.88-2.96]; 5 to <50 mGy: HR, 1.86 [95% CI, 1.16-2.81]; 50 to <75 mGy: HR, 2.30 [95% CI, 1.64-3.12]; 75 to <100 mGy: HR, 2.02 [95% CI, 1.13-3.30]; 100 to <150 mGy: HR, 2.81 [95% CI, 1.53-4.66]; ≥150 mGy: HR, 3.85 [95% CI, 2.43-5.75]). Cumulative dose was associated with brain tumor risk overall (ERR per 100 mGy, 1.27 [95% CI, 0.83-1.77]; P < .001), with stronger associations for aggressive histologies (ERR per 100 mGy, 1.51 [95% CI, 1.00-2.11]; P < .001). By age 21 years, exposure comparable to 1 head CT was associated with 7.9 excess brain tumors per 10 000 children, or approximately 1 excess tumor per 1266 head CT examinations. The estimated population-attributable fraction was 10.1% (95% CI, 5.8%-14.2%). Medical imaging in children and adolescents was associated with a dose-related increase in brain tumor risk. These findings support careful clinical justification and dose minimization when pediatric imaging using ionizing radiation is indicated.

papers.abstract: CAR-T cells have yet to show widespread efficacy in solid tumors due in part to poor persistence and dysfunction in the tumor microenvironment. Further, heterogenous expression of target antigens can lead to escape of antigen-null tumors that resist CAR-T killing. Strategies to cooperatively boost both CAR-T and endogenous antitumor immunity may be critical for achieving durable efficacy in cancer patients. NKTR-255 is a polymer-conjugated IL-15 with extended half-life that can boost endogenous T and NK cells, as well as CD19 CAR-T cells in B cell malignancies. However, whether NKTR-255 is sufficient to overcome CAR-T dysfunction in the suppressive solid tumor microenvironment, and how NKTR-255 and CAR-Ts together re-shape endogenous antitumor immunity, is not known. Using mouse models of ROR1+ lung adenocarcinoma, we show that NKTR-255 significantly boosted accumulation and function of tumor-infiltrating CAR-T cells targeting ROR1. Compared with NKTR-255 or CAR-T treatment alone, combination of NKTR-255 and CAR-T therapy increased endogenous tumor-specific T cells that preserved a PD-1+Tcf1+ stem-like phenotype. Consequently, NKTR-255 and CAR-T combination therapy completely eliminated ROR1+ tumor cells and significantly improved survival, with enhanced tumor control dependent on both CAR-Ts and endogenous T cells, though all mice ultimately succumbed to progression of ROR1- tumor. Compared to IL-15-armored CAR-T cells, systemic NKTR-255 induced greater accumulation and reduced terminal differentiation of endogenous tumor-specific T cells, resulting in superior tumor control. Thus, combining NKTR-255 with CAR-T therapy is a promising strategy to enhance both CAR-T and endogenous antitumor immunity to promote coordinated control of aggressive tumors.

papers.abstract: Cancer stem cells (CSC) are a small group of tumor cells capable of self-renewing, giving rise to new tumors, and resisting treatment, thereby causing recurrence and metastasis and representing a serious clinical problem. However, there are no approved therapies for their elimination, and limited information is available on the effects of current therapies on tumor stemness. A general consensus suggests that the anti-inflammatory and immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment promotes tumor stemness. Since we previously reported that ablation of the p50 NF-κB gene in the hematopoietic compartment (p50fl/flTie2-Cre mice) restores M1/Th1 antitumor immunity, we studied its effects on CSC and therapy resistance in models of fibrosarcoma and melanoma. Using p50fl/flTie2-Cre mice, we demonstrate that p50 NF-κB silencing impairs CSC development, their migratory capacity, and epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT), events known to correlate with tumor aggressiveness. Furthermore, we identify a clear antagonistic effect between Th1 and Th2 T cell polarization, with the former acting as inhibitors and the latter promoting the stemness phenotype. Consistently, while immunotherapy with anti-PD-1 promoted a marked reduction in CSC and tumor development, associated with increased levels of IFNγ, whereas concomitant administration of anti-IFNγ antibodies restored tumor growth and dissemination. Moreover, treatment with anti-IL-4 enhanced the antitumor effects of immunotherapy, reducing tumor cell stemness. Importantly, the antitumor effects of high-dose IFNγ and anti-IL-4 were confirmed in combination with doxorubicin chemotherapy. Overall, our data indicate that shifting the immune response toward a robust M1/Th1 state can significantly improve current immunotherapies and chemotherapies, by limiting CSC properties.

papers.abstract: Long-term lung cancer (LC) survivors remain at risk of LC events (LCEs), including late recurrence and second primary LC, beyond 5 years after diagnosis, but the role of computed tomography (CT) surveillance beyond 5 years remains uncertain. To evaluate whether CT receipt beyond 5 years after LC diagnosis is associated with LCEs and survival. This nationwide population-based cohort study used sequential target trial emulation with monthly eligibility reassessment and time-updated propensity score matching based on data from the Korean National Health Insurance Service database. Patients diagnosed with LC from 2006 to 2019 were followed up through December 31, 2024. Long-term LC survivors were eligible for trial entry 5.5 years after diagnosis if they had no administrative evidence of active or recurrent LC, a prior LCE, or another primary cancer. Data were analyzed between January 1, 2026, and February 28, 2026. CT receipt beyond 5 years after LC diagnosis, defined as chest CT during the 1-month assessment window at each monthly trial baseline, compared with no CT receipt. The primary outcome was LCE occurrence, defined by new LC-specific special copayment registration after the monthly trial baseline. Secondary outcomes were all-cause mortality, surgical resection after LCE detection, and subsequent mortality. The cohort of 55 694 LC survivors (mean [SD] age, 63.3 [10.9] years; 58.0% male) contributed 2 629 462 eligible person-trials. Matching yielded 583 756 person-trials per group. During a median (IQR) follow-up of 2.74 (1.16-5.18) years, CT receipt was associated with a higher incidence of LCEs (2.49% vs 1.97% per year; hazard ratio [HR], 1.28 [95% CI, 1.26-1.29]) and lower all-cause mortality rate (2.62% vs 4.33% per year; HR, 0.66 [95% CI, 0.65-0.67]) compared with no CT receipt. Among patients with an LCE, CT receipt was associated with greater odds of surgical resection after LCE (odds ratio, 1.46 [95% CI, 1.41-1.52]) and a lower subsequent mortality risk (HR, 0.63 [95% CI, 0.61-0.64]). These associations were observed more frequently among females (HR, 0.47 [95% CI, 0.44-0.49]), older adults (HR, 0.57 [95% CI, 0.54-0.60]), and never smokers (HR, 0.55 [95% CI, 0.53-0.57]). In this cohort study, CT receipt beyond 5 years after LC diagnosis was associated with increased detection of LCEs, greater use of surgical resection after an LCE, and a lower all-cause mortality rate. These findings support further evaluation of risk-adapted CT surveillance beyond 5 years in selected LC survivors.

papers.abstract: Lung cancer screening with low-dose computed tomography (LDCT) has been shown to identify lung cancers at earlier stages and to significantly reduce lung cancer mortality in prior randomized clinical trials. However, the benefit of LDCT screening for small cell lung cancer (SCLC), an aggressive subtype of lung cancer, is unclear. To investigate the characteristics and outcomes of SCLC diagnosed after a lung cancer screening examination using a large database of Medicare beneficiaries. In this retrospective cohort study, Medicare data linked to the Surveillance Epidemiology End Results Program's cancer registry data were analyzed. Patients in the US aged 65 to 78 years who were diagnosed with SCLC from 2015 to 2021 were identified for analysis, with follow-up data through 2022. Patients who underwent 1 or more LDCT lung cancer screening examinations during the 12 months preceding their SCLC diagnosis were included in the screened group. All other patients were included in the unscreened group. Data were analyzed from January to August 2026. One or more LDCT lung cancer screenings during the 12 months preceding SCLC diagnosis. The primary outcomes were stage at SCLC diagnosis and overall survival after SCLC diagnosis in the screened and unscreened groups. A total of 17 099 patients (median [IQR] age, 72.0 [69.0-75.0] years; 8999 [52.6%] female) met study inclusion criteria, of which 949 (5.5%) were included in the screened group and 16 150 (94.5%) were included in the unscreened group. When compared with patients in the unscreened group, patients in the screened group were significantly less likely to be diagnosed with distant disease (419 of 949 [44.2%] vs 11 376 of 16 150 [70.4%]; P < .001). Patients in the screened group also had significantly better overall survival when compared with patients in the unscreened group (3-year overall survival, 28.0% [95% CI, 24.9%-31.2%] vs 10.8% [95% CI, 10.3%-11.3%]; P < .001). Both findings were consistent in propensity score-matched analysis. Results of this cohort study of Medicare beneficiaries diagnosed with SCLC suggest that receipt of lung cancer screening was associated with a shift toward earlier-stage SCLC at diagnosis and improved overall survival.

papers.abstract: NRG Oncology RTOG 9902 was a randomized controlled trial of the addition of adjuvant chemotherapy (paclitaxel, oral etoposide, estramustine) to long-course androgen suppression and radiation for patients with high-risk prostate cancer. The trial closed early due to excess toxicity and found no benefit to chemotherapy at a median follow-up of 9.2 years. Immediate post-radiation PSA status was dichotomized at ≤ 0.2 ng/mL. Landmark analysis redefined starting times for disease-free survival (DFS), time to distant metastasis (TDM), and overall survival (OS) at 36 weeks post-radiation, when planned chemotherapy was complete. Exclusion criteria included non-receipt of radiation or assigned chemotherapy and pre-landmark DFS events or loss to follow-up. Hazard ratios (HR), 95% confidence intervals, and PSA-by-treatment interaction estimated by Cox or competing-risks regression. Of 333 patients analyzed: 190 without and 143 with chemotherapy. Chemotherapy was associated with improved DFS for patients with PSA > 0.2 (HR 0.59, 0.38-0.91), but not for those with PSA ≤ 0.2 (HR 0.94, 0.60-1.46), interaction p = 0.13. There was no association with chemotherapy relative to post-RT PSA for either TDM or OS. This analysis suggests that men with a post-radiation PSA > 0.2 may benefit from treatment intensification with adjuvant chemotherapy. Prospective trials adapting treatment by PSA response are indicated. Trial Number: NCT00004054 (ClinicalTrials.gov).

papers.abstract: Insulin-like growth factor (IGF) signaling drives progression of glioblastoma (GBM), the most aggressive brain cancer. While sphingolipid metabolism is implicated in gliomagenesis, the mechanism by which it regulates GBM growth and therapy response is poorly understood. Through bioinformatic analyses of human gliomas, we identified sphingolipid metabolism genes with potential functional significance in glioma. Using patient-derived cells, a Drosophila glioma model, and xenograft mouse models, we investigated the functional role of Dihydroceramide desaturase 1 (DEGS1). Lipidomics profiling and RNA sequencing were performed in patient-derived cells to reveal the mechanism by which DEGS1 regulates glioma growth. Additionally, we tested the effect of a DEGS1 inhibitor on GBM cell growth and their resistance to IGF1R-targeted therapy. Our data demonstrate that the expression of sphingolipid metabolism gene DEGS1 is associated with aggressive glioma biomarkers and worse patient survival. DEGS1 is required for glioma growth in patient-derived cells, a Drosophila glioma model, and xenograft mouse models. Lipidomics profiling reveals that DEGS1 deficiency results in reduced ceramides and complex sphingolipids and accumulation of their precursors. Disrupted sphingolipid homeostasis impairs lipid raft biogenesis and lipid raft-associated IGF signaling. Targeting DEGS1 decreases GBM cell growth and their resistance to IGF1R inhibition. These findings establish that targeting DEGS1-regulated sphingolipid metabolism is a viable avenue to inhibit IGF signaling-driven GBM growth.

papers.abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) develops in a nutrient-poor microenvironment and progresses from pancreatic intraepithelial neoplasia (PanIN) to invasive carcinoma. Serine metabolism supports tumor growth in many cancers, spurring the development of inhibitors of phosphoglycerate dehydrogenase (PHGDH), the rate-limiting enzyme in serine biosynthesis. However, the limited clinical success of PHGDH inhibitors highlights the need to better understand the stage-specific role of de novo serine synthesis during PDAC progression. Here, we showed that PHGDH increases progressively from PanIN to invasive PDAC in human and mouse tissues. In genetically engineered mouse models with inducible PHGDH knockdown, PHGDH loss delayed PDAC development. Acute treatment with the PHGDH inhibitor BI-9593 suppressed de novo serine synthesis, induced cell death, and drove tumor regression. Unexpectedly, PHGDH-deficient tumors did not become more dependent on exogenous serine, and dietary serine/glycine manipulation did not affect tumor development. Instead, stable isotope tracing and metabolomic profiling showed that PHGDH loss reduced ASCT2 expression and impaired glutamine uptake and utilization, creating a metabolic liability that rendered PHGDH-deficient tumors selectively sensitive to the glutamine antagonist DRP-104. Together, these findings reveal a therapeutic vulnerability to combined metabolic targeting in PDAC.

papers.abstract: Tissue injury is a pervasive feature of human disease, yet adult mammals exhibit limited regenerative capacity. A central determinant of regenerative outcomes is the inflammatory response, which orchestrates tissue repair through mechanisms that are evolutionarily conserved from Drosophila to mammals. Following injury, inflammation drives debris clearance, promotes the release of cytokines and growth factors, and contributes to the restoration of functional cells. However, dysregulated or unresolved inflammation can impair healing, drive scar formation, and ultimately result in organ dysfunction or failure. Here, we focus on recent advances in the spatiotemporal regulation of inflammation during tissue repair that have reshaped our understanding of its underlying mechanisms. We synthesize findings on the dynamic progression of repair from inflammatory initiation to active resolution and stem cell activation, highlighting features of immune cell plasticity and heterogeneity within injury-specific microenvironments, as well as the existence of pivotal macrophage-fibroblast interactions. Furthermore, we delineate the pleiotropic and context-dependent roles of key cytokines and signaling pathways in coordinating these processes. Finally, we discuss current and emerging therapeutic strategies, emphasizing the paradigm shift from broad immunosuppression toward precise modulation of inflammatory networks to promote regeneration and prevent fibrosis. Future progress hinges on integrating multiomic spatial atlases, precision immunomodulation, and standardized therapeutic protocols to decipher and manipulate immune-regenerative crosstalk, thereby driving the development of next-generation regenerative therapies.

papers.abstract: Accurate prediction of treatment response remains challenging in cancer. To facilitate response prediction in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), we developed PRISM, an interpretable multiscale graph-learning framework for estimating treatment-specific objective response from pretreatment H&E whole-slide images. PRISM integrated multiresolution tissue representations with a cell-level tumor microenvironment (TME) hypergraph, thereby treating higher-order microenvironmental organization as a learnable component of treatment-response prediction. Samples from 7,082 patients from four Chinese centers were screened. PRISM was evaluated across treatment specific cohorts receiving targeted therapy (T), EGFR-targeted therapy (T_EGFR), immune checkpoint inhibitor-based therapy (ICI), chemoimmunotherapy (CI), and chemotherapy (C) using patient-level internal cross-validation, independent multicenter external validation, and prospective silent validation. PRISM predicted early objective responses across prespecified systemic therapies in NSCLC. In comparison to 18 established multiple-instance learning and computational pathology baseline models, PRISM remained competitive, with numerical advantages in selected tasks. Multiscale attribution and exploratory H&E-derived TME analyses provided spatial context for model predictions. Overall, PRISM offers a morphology-based framework for estimating early response to prespecified systemic therapies and warrants further prospective multicenter evaluation.

papers.abstract: Resistance to PD-1-based immunotherapy remains a major challenge in cancer treatment, especially in immunologically "cold" tumors characterized by T-cell exclusion and impaired T-cell effector function. Mechanical processes impact T-cell activity, and mechanical perturbations may represent a distinct mode of immune suppression. Here, we identified CD209, a myeloid-expressed C-type lectin receptor, as a mechanosuppressive regulator of antitumor T-cell immunity. CD209 was selectively enriched in tumor-infiltrating M2-like macrophages and monocytes, and elevated CD209 expression was associated with poor clinical response to PD-1 blockade and immune dysfunction and exclusion across multiple cancer types. Mechanistically, CD209 directly engaged ICAM-2 on T cells and activated ROCK1-ERM signaling. This interaction increased T-cell cortical stiffness, destabilized T cell-antigen presenting cell interactions, and attenuated T-cell receptor signaling. Blocking the CD209-ICAM-2-ERM pathway restored T-cell activation and promoted CD8+ T-cell infiltration and effector function in both in vivo mouse models and ex vivo human tumor systems. Importantly, CD209 blockade enhanced the response to PD-1 inhibition and overcame resistance to PD-1-based immunotherapy in refractory and immunologically "cold" tumor models. Together, these findings define a myeloid-derived mechanical immune checkpoint and reveal T-cell mechanosuppression as a targetable mechanism of tumor immune evasion and immunotherapy resistance.

papers.abstract: Functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) measures cortical hemodynamics, yet its ability to characterize anesthesia-related functional changes remains unclear. This exploratory secondary analysis used prospectively collected data from 120 female patients undergoing gynecologic laparoscopic surgery under propofol or sevoflurane anesthesia (60 per group). Twenty-channel prefrontal fNIRS recordings covered wakefulness, induction, and maintenance. Deoxygenated hemoglobin-derived amplitude of low-frequency fluctuations (ALFF), functional connectivity (FC), network topology, and within- and cross-state FC similarity were assessed. Support vector machine, logistic regression, and random forest classifiers assessed discrimination between states. During induction, ALFF increased by 89.8% to 202.2% with propofol and 75.2% to 242.0% with sevoflurane across five prefrontal regions (all P < 0.001). During maintenance, mean ALFF was below awake levels, with significant reductions of 20.0% to 40.1% in three regions under sevoflurane (all P ≤ 0.019). Induction-related FC changes were limited and regionally heterogeneous. Regional FC, modularity, and global efficiency showed no significant maintenance-versus-awake differences in either group. Within-state between-subject FC similarity was significantly higher during maintenance than during wakefulness only with sevoflurane (mean difference [MD], 0.110; 95% CI, 0.054 to 0.169; P < 0.001). Cross-state between-subject FC similarity was higher for awake-maintenance than awake-induction comparisons with propofol (MD, 0.072; 95% CI, 0.055 to 0.090) and sevoflurane (MD, 0.144; 95% CI, 0.126 to 0.161; both P < 0.001). Support vector machine classification of induction versus wakefulness yielded areas under the curve (AUCs) of 0.83 (95% CI, 0.75 to 0.90) for propofol and 0.85 (95% CI, 0.78 to 0.91) for sevoflurane; maintenance-versus-awake AUCs were 0.67 (95% CI, 0.58 to 0.75) and 0.76 (95% CI, 0.68 to 0.85). Prefrontal fNIRS detected widespread induction-related hemodynamic changes, but the present connectivity measures provided limited discrimination between maintenance of anesthesia and wakefulness.

papers.abstract: Cancer-like genetic variants threaten bioreactor expansion of human pluripotent stem cells (hPSCs) for cell therapy manufacturing. papers.abstract: Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) have transformed the treatment landscape of head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC). In the recurrent/metastatic (R/M) setting, pembrolizumab has been approved as first-line therapy, either alone for tumors with PD-L1 combined positive score (CPS) ≥ 1 or in combination with platinum-based chemotherapy regardless of PD-L1 CPS status. Moreover, both pembrolizumab and nivolumab have been approved as monotherapy in platinum-refractory disease. More recently, perioperative pembrolizumab received U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approval for resectable, locally advanced HNSCC with PD-L1 CPS ≥ 1 following encouraging results of the KEYNOTE-689 trial. Although PD-L1 CPS is the only validated HNSCC-specific biomarker for immunotherapy selection, its accuracy remains limited, as response rates are modest even among PD-L1 CPS-high patients, while some tumors with low/negative CPS may still derive benefit. This underscores the need for novel biomarkers with greater predictive value that can serve as more precise selection and risk stratification tools for patients with HNSCC considering immunotherapy. Recent studies have investigated several biomarkers of immunotherapy outcomes in HNSCC in both tissue and blood, paving the way toward adopting non-invasive approaches. In this review, we aim to summarize recent advances in ICI biomarker discovery in non-nasopharyngeal HNSCC and to set the basis for the adoption of an integrated approach, comprising both tissue-based and liquid biomarkers.

papers.abstract: Gastrointestinal (GI) cancers have been a largely disappointing arena for immune-checkpoint inhibition, with durable benefit confined to mismatch-repair-deficient (dMMR/MSI-H) disease, PD-L1-enriched gastroesophageal adenocarcinoma, and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). A shared feature of many resistant GI tumors is a vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF)-driven, immune-excluded microenvironment, providing a mechanistic rationale for co-targeting angiogenesis and the PD-(L)1 axis. The clinical foundation for this strategy has now been established across GI malignancies: atezolizumab plus bevacizumab became standard of care in HCC (IMbrave150), and the combination of zanzalintinib with atezolizumab delivered the first immune-checkpoint-based overall-survival benefit in microsatellite-stable (MSS) colorectal cancer in the phase 3 STELLAR-303 trial - providing phase 3 support for multikinase (VEGFR/MET/TAM-family)/checkpoint co-targeting in a disease long considered immune-refractory, and supporting the VEGF/checkpoint hypothesis without establishing that the benefit is attributable to VEGF-pathway inhibition specifically. These successes have catalyzed the development of single-molecule VEGF/VEGFR × PD-1/PD-L1 bispecific antibodies, which aim to consolidate and potentially improve upon the co-targeting paradigm through cooperative binding, conditional tumor selectivity, and simplified pharmacology. Ivonescimab (AK112) is the most clinically advanced agent and carries the broadest GI portfolio, spanning colorectal, gastroesophageal, hepatobiliary, and pancreatic programs; pumitamig (BNT327/PM8002) and SSGJ-707 (PF-08634404) anchor parallel registrational efforts. In biliary tract cancer, the randomized phase 3 HARMONi-GI1 trial - presented at ESMO 2026 - showed that ivonescimab plus gemcitabine/cisplatin improved overall survival over durvalumab plus gemcitabine/cisplatin (median 14.9 versus 12.1 months; HR 0.75), the first positive phase 3 result for the class in a GI cancer, albeit from an interim analysis in a China-only population with benefit confined to intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma; the remaining pivotal programs (HARMONi-GI2/GI3, ROSETTA) are ongoing. The biological warrant and cross-tumor signals are compelling, but GI-specific efficacy and safety for the bispecific class remain early, geographically concentrated, and confounded by comparator choice; no bispecific-validated biomarker yet exists. HARMONi-GI1 establishes superiority over checkpoint-plus-chemotherapy in one disease; the trials now needed are those comparing the bispecific with the co-administered anti-VEGF/checkpoint doublet, which alone can determine whether single-molecule co-targeting delivers a genuinely immunological gain or merely a superior anti-angiogenic effect.

papers.abstract: Pediatric B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (B-ALL) remains a major clinical challenge driven by molecular heterogeneity and therapeutic resistance. While the SWI/SNF chromatin-remodeling complex is a recognized dependency in myeloid and T-cell leukemias, its role in B-ALL remains poorly defined. Here, we identify a conserved requirement for the SWI/SNF ATPases SMARCA4 and SMARCA2 across diverse B-ALL genetic subtypes. SMARCA4 expression correlates with inferior overall survival in the pediatric B-ALL TARGET cohort. Using a panel of B-ALL models representing ETV6-RUNX1, BCR-ABL1, and KMT2A-rearranged subtypes, we show that dual SMARCA2/4 inhibition, using the ATPase inhibitor BRM014 or the PROTAC degrader ACBI1, induces profound loss of viability. This vulnerability is characterized by G0/G1 cell cycle arrest and a robust apoptotic response. Mechanistically, comparative RNA sequencing identified a high-confidence 26-gene "identity core" consistently downregulated upon SWI/SNF disruption with BRM014. This program integrates lymphocyte activation, cytokine signaling, and trafficking modules, including the key niche-interaction receptor CXCR4, and is accompanied by depletion of MYC and E2F transcriptional programs. Finally, BRM014 demonstrated significant growth-inhibitory activity in vivo in an REH xenograft model, with a significant delay in disease progression during the observation window. These findings establish the SWI/SNF complex as a conserved survival dependency in the tested B-ALL models and provide a rationale for targeting SMARCA2/4 to inhibit intrinsic growth in B-ALL.

papers.abstract: Brain neoplasms cause substantial morbidity and mortality in low- and middle-income countries, yet structural and geographic factors in access and outcomes are poorly quantified. Using discharge data from Mexico's Ministry of Health hospitals, we examined access to brain tumor surgery and the relationship between facility level and mortality. We retrospectively analyzed patients undergoing brain tumor surgery in Ministry of Health hospitals using the national discharge registry (2010-2022). Multivariable logistic regression with hospital-clustered standard errors assessed associations of facility level and travel time with in-hospital mortality, adjusting for clinical and socioeconomic covariates. We also examined timely access among patients and in the population. Among 10,532 patients, 74.4% reached care within 2 h, and 68.0% of the population lived within 2 h of a Ministry of Health level 3 neurosurgical center, below the 80% Lancet Commission benchmark. Indigenous community, pediatric age, and male sex were associated with lower odds of timely access. Surgery at a level 2 versus level 3 hospital was associated with higher in-hospital mortality (OR 1.25; 95% CI 1.01-1.56; sensitivity range 1.22-1.40), and travel time, less consistently, with a modest increase (OR 1.04 per hour beyond 2 h; 95% CI 1.00-1.07). Malignancy, older age, and pediatric age were associated with higher mortality. Within Mexico's Ministry of Health hospitals, brain tumor surgery is geographically concentrated, and surgery at level 2 hospitals was associated with higher in-hospital mortality. These findings warrant evaluation of level 2 neurosurgical capacity and referral pathways to tertiary centers.

papers.abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) remains a leading cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide, largely due to tumor heterogeneity, late diagnosis, and high recurrence rates even after curative treatment. Although HCC is potentially curable when detected at an early stage, suboptimal surveillance, particularly in patients with underlying cirrhosis or metabolic risk factors, limits the proportion of patients eligible for curative therapies. Current surveillance strategies for at-risk populations have intrinsic limitations, and the performance of imaging and serum biomarkers remains suboptimal. Moreover, the lack of reliable prognostic biomarkers for detecting early recurrence hampers post-treatment surveillance and impacts clinical outcomes. In this context, circulating biomarkers have emerged as promising tools for improving both early detection and prognostic stratification. Liquid biopsy has the potential to enable early, non-invasive diagnosis of HCC and allows longitudinal assessment of tumor progression through serial sampling. In early-stage HCC, blood candidates may complement or outperform conventional approaches by enabling earlier diagnosis and more accurate risk stratification. In this review, we summarize recent advances and current challenges in the clinical translation of circulating biomarkers. We focus on key liquid biopsy components, including circulating cell-free DNA, particularly circulating tumor DNA, circulating tumor cells, non-coding RNAs, extracellular vesicles, proteins and metabolites, such as bile acids and lipids, highlighting their diagnostic and prognostic potential and their possible integration into personalized management strategies for patients with early-stage HCC.

papers.abstract: Cancer incidence continues to increase globally, with many patients diagnosed during working age. Employment disruption after cancer diagnosis is an important survivorship and socioeconomic issue, yet long-term evidence across cancer types and patient subgroups remains limited. This study evaluated unemployment risk and workforce attrition among workers after cancer diagnosis. We conducted a nationwide cohort study of workers aged 18 to 60 years newly diagnosed with cancer between 2011 and 2020, with follow-up of up to 12 years. Noncancer workers were selected using 1:1 hybrid matching based on demographic, clinical, and insurance characteristics. The primary outcome was unemployment, defined as transition from employee status to dependent or local administrative enrollment without dependent eligibility for at least 12 months. Workforce attrition, defined as unemployment or death, was evaluated as a secondary outcome. Competing risk and Cox regression models were applied. After matching, 119,200 pairs of cancer and noncancer workers were included. The cumulative incidence of unemployment among cancer workers was 7.9% at 1 year and 32.5% at 12 years, compared with 5.3% and 22.9% among noncancer workers. Cancer diagnosis was associated with higher unemployment risk (subdistribution hazard ratio, 1.51; 95% CI, 1.48 to 1.54). Risks were greatest among women, individuals aged 40 to 49 years, and those with advanced-stage disease. Cancer was also associated with an approximately threefold higher risk of workforce attrition. Cancer diagnosis was associated with substantial long-term employment disruption. These findings highlight the need for survivorship-oriented workforce support and employment protection strategies.

papers.abstract: Tailgut cysts are rare congenital retrorectal lesions. Because the risk of malignancy remains uncertain, resection has historically been recommended even for asymptomatic patients. We examined whether clinical and imaging features can identify patients suitable for active surveillance. Patients diagnosed with a tailgut cyst at a tertiary cancer center between 1996 and 2021 were identified from radiology and pathology databases. Demographic, clinical, imaging, operative, pathologic, and oncologic data were reviewed. Management was individualized after multidisciplinary review. Survival was estimated using the Kaplan-Meier method. Fifty-four patients were included; 47 (87%) had benign disease and 7 (13%) had malignant disease. Malignancy was present at diagnosis in all cases and occurred exclusively in symptomatic patients. Malignancy was associated with older age (median 57 vs. 45 years, p = 0.036) and rectal pain at presentation (86% vs. 30%, p = 0.008). On imaging, malignant cysts were significantly larger and more likely to demonstrate solid components, calcifications, and adjacent structure involvement. Twenty patients with benign-appearing cysts were enrolled in active surveillance. In this cohort, no malignant events were observed during follow-up, with a 5-year cancer-free survival of 100%. Five-year overall survival was 28.6% for malignant versus 91.9% for benign cysts (p < 0.0001). Malignant tailgut cysts appear to represent a clinically and radiographically distinct subset present at diagnosis. Asymptomatic patients with benign-appearing cysts demonstrated excellent long-term outcomes under active surveillance. These findings suggest that a risk-adapted management strategy incorporating symptoms and imaging features may help guide selection between surgery and surveillance.

papers.abstract: While nanomedicines hold great promise for solid tumour therapy, their penetration and access to tumour cells is limited by large glycosylated proteins called mucins that are enriched in the tumour microenvironment. Here we show that mucins induce the disassembly of self-assembled mPEG-polyester micellar nanoparticles into smaller unimers. Leveraging this finding, we designed a mucin-responsive, paclitaxel-conjugated nanomedicine (mrPNM) whose unimers are capable of escaping the mucin-binding barrier. Following intravenous injection, this designer mucin-responsive nanomedicine exhibited markedly deeper penetration than the mucin-nonresponsive nanomedicine and albumin, resulting in 3.9- and 1.5-fold increases in tumour cell delivery, respectively, in a pancreatic mouse tumour model. The mrPNMs also achieved superior tumour growth inhibition compared to both the mucin-nonresponsive nanomedicine and Abraxane, the FDA-approved nanoparticle albumin-bound paclitaxel, in three solid tumour models. The mucin-responsive nanomedicine platform could provide a general strategy for improving the treatment of solid tumours.

papers.abstract: Aneuploidy and chromosomal instability are common characteristics of cancer but remain underexploited therapeutically. Chromosomally unstable cells are often selectively vulnerable to inhibition of the kinesin KIF18A, and this dependence is related to altered mitotic control. Here, we identify the spindle and kinetochore-associated (SKA) complex as a mitotic regulator that establishes a similar dependency. SKA complex loss is tolerated in cells with a defective mitotic checkpoint, but when mitosis is prolonged, it leads to mitotic errors and loss of viability. Genetic analysis reveals that the SKA complex and KIF18A are epistatic, although they function through mechanistically distinct mitotic pathways. SKA complex depletion selectively impacts chromosomally unstable cancer cells and mirrors the effects of KIF18A inhibition. We thus identify a cellular vulnerability associated with prolonged mitosis in chromosomally unstable cancers.

papers.abstract: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) is characterized by pronounced molecular heterogeneity and remains incurable in a substantial fraction of patients who relapse or develop refractory disease following standard chemoimmunotherapy. PIM kinases are constitutively active oncogenic serine/threonine kinases implicated in lymphoma pathogenesis, transcriptional control and cell viability. However, the detailed molecular mechanisms by which PIMs regulate transcriptional programs, RNA metabolism, and genome stability remain largely unknown. Here, we demonstrate that PIM kinases maintain interphase phosphorylation of histone H3 at serine 10 (H3S10ph). Genetic or pharmacological inhibition of PIM kinase family leads to a global reduction of H3S10ph and other active histone marks, impaired RNA polymerase II elongation, and widespread transcriptional repression. Integrated epigenomic and transcriptomic analyses reveal that PIM family inhibition preferentially affects gene networks involved in RNA metabolism, including RNA processing, splicing, and RNA methylation pathways. PIM1 proximity proteome analysis identified multiple splicing-related proteins, and PIM1 co-association with SF3B1, XAB2, and EDC3 was confirmed using co-immunoprecipitation. Functionally, PIM kinase inhibition induces extensive alternative mRNA splicing abnormalities, promotes the accumulation of RNA-DNA hybrids (R-loops), and triggers DNA damage-associated checkpoint responses. Consistent with these findings, in preliminary in vitro drug combination studies, PIM inhibition synergizes with DNA-damaging chemotherapy and targeted inhibitors of the DNA damage response. Collectively, our results implicate PIM kinases in the regulation of transcription, RNA metabolism, and genome stability in DLBCL and provide a preclinical rationale for further investigation of combinations of PIM inhibitors with DNA-damaging agents or DNA damage response inhibitors.

papers.abstract: Myelodysplastic neoplasms (MDS) are clonal myeloid neoplasms characterized by ineffective hematopoiesis, cytopenias, and a variable risk of transformation to Acute myeloid leukemia (AML). Although genetic lesions are central to MDS pathogenesis, progression to AML cannot be explained by mutation accumulation alone. This review synthesizes evidence that MDS-to-AML transformation is a dynamic ecological process driven by reciprocal interactions between mutant hematopoietic stem and progenitor cell clones and the bone marrow immune microenvironment. In normal marrow, hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells, T cells, NK(natural killer) cells, myeloid cells, mesenchymal stromal cells, endothelial cells, and the extracellular matrix maintain hematopoietic homeostasis and immune surveillance. In MDS, chronic inflammation coexists with impaired immune effector function, including T-cell exhaustion, reduced NK-cell cytotoxicity, expansion of myeloid-derived suppressor cells and immunosuppressive regulatory T-cell subsets, monocyte-macrophage reprogramming, mesenchymal stromal cell dysfunction, extracellular matrix remodeling, and metabolic adaptation. Together, these alterations establish a proinflammatory but immunosuppressive niche that weakens clearance of abnormal clones while providing stromal and metabolic support for clonal expansion and treatment resistance. Mutant clones further remodel the niche through epigenetic silencing, altered chemokine and cytokine signaling, and inflammatory-metabolic reprogramming, generating positive-feedback circuits that link inflammation, DNA damage, immune escape, increasing clonal burden, and therapy resistance. This review discusses how integrating clonal genetics with immune, stromal, and metabolic features may refine risk stratification and inform microenvironment-directed combination therapies. Longitudinal single-cell and spatial profiling will be essential for identifying reversible immune dysfunction and developing individualized strategies to delay or prevent AML transformation.

papers.abstract: Intervertebral disc degeneration (IDD) lacks effective disease-modifying therapy. This study evaluated the protective effects of irbesartan (Ir), explored fibroblast growth factor receptor 1 (FGFR1) as a candidate molecular mediator, and assessed whether cRGD modification could enhance nanoparticle uptake and local treatment effects. Rat IDD models and IL-1β-induced degenerative nucleus pulposus cells were used to assess free Ir and Ir-loaded cRGD-modified PLGA nanoparticles (cRGD-NPs@Ir). Bioinformatics screening, cellular thermal shift assay (CETSA), and molecular docking were used to nominate FGFR1 as a candidate Ir-associated protein, and FGFR1 knockdown was used to test whether FGFR1 status modified the treatment response. Imaging, histology, immunohistochemistry, Western blotting, RT-qPCR, nanoparticle characterization, Coumarin-6 uptake assays, and tandem LC3 reporter analysis were used to evaluate treatment-associated changes. Ir attenuated structural and molecular features of IDD, reduced MAPK/NF-κB signaling, altered autophagy-associated markers, and preserved extracellular matrix homeostasis. FGFR1 expression was lower in degenerative disc tissue, and FGFR1 knockdown attenuated several protective changes associated with Ir or cRGD-NPs@Ir. cRGD-NPs@Ir produced greater carrier-associated Coumarin-6 uptake than NPs@Ir and larger treatment-associated changes than free Ir for several directly compared endpoints. These findings support an FGFR1-related component of the response but do not establish direct Ir-FGFR1 binding, receptor-specific cRGD targeting, or exclusive FGFR1 dependence. FGFR1 may contribute as a candidate molecular mediator to Ir-associated changes in autophagy and inflammatory signaling in IDD. cRGD-NPs@Ir provides an uptake-enhancing local nanodelivery strategy, although receptor specificity and direct Ir-FGFR1 binding require further validation.

papers.abstract: A comprehensive understanding of the Ras self-inactivation mechanism at atomic resolution-specifically, intrinsic GTP hydrolysis converting the GTP-bound active form to the GDP-bound inactive form-is essential for designing therapies against Ras-driven cancers. Conventional models describe a biphasic GTP-bound state: Ras interconverts between inactive state 1 and active, catalytically competent state 2. However, the structural pathway leading to Ras/GDP via these states remains unclear. Here, we use time-resolved serial femtosecond and synchrotron crystallography to capture GTP hydrolysis in Ras crystals loaded with photoactivatable caged GTP, across timescales from milliseconds to hours. Photolysis yielded Ras in state 1-a conformation lacking a stabilized nucleophilic water characteristic of state 2. Remarkably, this state persists for hours and converts directly to Ras/GDP without passing through state 2. These findings challenge the prevailing view that state 2 is essential and suggest that state 1 can directly support catalysis, offering an alternative conceptual basis for targeting clinically relevant Ras mutants that preferentially adopt this conformation.

papers.abstract: Ultrasound-guided radial artery cannulation is common in pediatrics but technically challenging. While the ulnar artery is a potential alternative, its sonoanatomy relative to the radial artery is not well defined. This study aimed to compare the sonoanatomic characteristics of the radial and ulnar arteries in children, evaluating how age, weight, and wrist position (0°, 30°, and 45°) influence arterial dimensions and depth to identify the most favorable profile for cannulation. Ultrasound evaluation of the radial and ulnar arteries was performed at 0°, 30°, and 45° wrist extension in 180 anesthetized children aged 0-120 months using custom-made wooden blocks. Arterial dimensions and skin-to-artery distance were evaluated overall and across age (≤ 24 vs. > 24 months) and weight (≤ 12 vs. > 12 kg) subgroups to identify optimal access conditions. Wrist extension angle did not significantly affect anteroposterior diameter (1.4 ± 0.3 mm, p = 0.078), but significantly influenced transverse arterial diameter (1.5-1.6 mm, p = 0.003) and skin-to-artery distance (2.4-2.8 mm at 30°, p < 0.001). The radial artery was widest at 0° (1.6 ± 1.0 mm), while the ulnar artery peaked at 30° (1.6 ± 0.4 mm). Skin-to-artery distance was minimized at 30° for both vessels. In children ≤ 12 kg, radial transverse diameter decreased paradoxically from 0° to 45° (1.6 ± 0.4 to 1.4 ± 0.3 mm, p = 0.013), while the ulnar artery was widest at 30° (1.5 ± 0.3 mm, p = 0.007). In infants ≤ 24 months, wrist angle did not significantly influence radial artery depth (p = 0.631, mean overall depth between 2.5-2.6 mm). A 30° wrist extension angle provides the most favorable sonoanatomic profile for both arteries. Although a larger vessel caliber may potentially facilitate cannulation, its clinical benefit remains uncertain as cannulation outcomes were not assessed. These findings support individualized ultrasound-guided assessment rather than a fixed positioning strategy.

papers.abstract: The prevalence of obesity is rising. Patients with obesity are increasingly exposed to anaesthesia, critical care, and perioperative pharmacotherapy. Obesity alters drug pharmacokinetics in a non-linear, drug-specific manner, so that simply scaling doses to total body weight (TBW) exposes patients to overdose or underdose. A recurring clinical question is therefore: which body weight descriptor should be used for which molecule? This review was conducted in accordance with the PRISMA extension for Scoping Reviews. We synthesized pharmacokinetic evidence, recent meta-analyses, and French and European guidelines on dose adjustment in adults with obesity for five drug classes of anaesthesia and critical care: hypnotics, opioids, neuromuscular blocking agents (NMBA), perioperative antibiotics, and non-opioid analgesics. We summarised the recommended dosing weight for each molecule in a table and a figure. No single weight descriptor applies. Lipophilic induction agents (propofol), most opioids (alfentanil, fentanyl, sufentanil), and non-depolarising NMBA are best dosed on lean or ideal body weight, whereas succinylcholine, neuromuscular reversal, and aminoglycosides use total or adjusted body weight. Maintenance of hypnosis and pain management in the post-anaesthesia care unit are titrated to monitored effect. Cephalosporin-based antibiotic prophylaxis relies on fixed doses (e.g., cefazolin 2 g) up to high body mass index values due to their hydrophilic properties. Paracetamol and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs are given at standard doses and never scaled to TBW. Findings are consolidated in a single bedside reference table. Dosing in obesity must be molecule-specific, guided by the relevant weight descriptor and by intraoperative monitoring rather than by TBW alone.

papers.abstract: The prognostic performance of the Simplified Acute Physiology Score (SAPS) models has not been thoroughly investigated. We systematically reviewed and meta-analysed SAPS mortality prediction metrics across diverse intensive care unit (ICU) populations worldwide. PubMed and Scopus were queried for external validations of SAPS in ICU settings. The "CHARMS" and "PROBAST" tools were applied for data extraction and risk-of-bias assessment, respectively. C-statistics and observed-to-expected ratios were summarised using random-effects models. Heterogeneity sources were explored using meta-regression. Evidence certainty was evaluated using the "GRADE" approach. PROSPERO registration CRD42023446721. Ninety studies (89 articles) were reviewed, totalling 565,994 ICU patients across 87 countries, and validating the SAPS II (n = 35), SAPS 3 global (n = 37), and/or SAPS 3 region-specific (n = 28) models. Endpoints were in-hospital (n = 70), in-ICU (n = 16), and/or 28/30-day mortality (n = 12). Nine studies performed recalibrations of SAPS II and 7 of SAPS 3. The meta-analyses provided high-certainty evidence of excellent discriminatory ability across all SAPS models in predicting in-hospital mortality, whereas data on unsatisfactory overall calibration were graded as low certainty. Successful recalibration was graded as high certainty for SAPS II and moderate certainty for SAPS 3. For ICU and 28/30-day mortality, the evidence was low to very low certainty for all SAPS models. Five decision curve analyses were conducted in three studies, all yielding positive net benefit across meaningful risk thresholds. SAPS models remain reliable as mortality risk-ranking tools in critical care. With adequate sample sizes, local recalibrations and dynamic updating of in-hospital mortality predictions are essential to ensure clinical utility. PROSPERO CRD42023446721.

papers.abstract: To update the evidence on neurological and respiratory predictors of extubation failure after acute brain injury and to compare the two families, as pre-specified. Five databases were searched through July 2026 for studies relating a predictor measured at or near extubation to extubation failure in ventilated adults with acute brain injury. Screening and extraction were done in duplicate; risk of bias was assessed using QUIPS. Adjusted estimates were pooled after harmonising outcome framing and predictor coding, restricting each pool to one scale and instrument, with random-effects (REML, Hartung-Knapp) and Bayesian hierarchical models. Certainty was assessed using GRADE. 98 studies (24 505 patients) yielded 415 predictor-outcome estimates; 194 carried a confidence interval, and 6 studies contributed to pooled adjusted estimates. Absent or weak cough was associated with failure (4 studies; OR 2.47, 95% CI 1.46-4.19; posterior median 2.55, 95% CrI 1.54-4.71, P(OR > 1) = 0.999; I² = 0%; moderate certainty), in line with the previous synthesis; in an illustrative projection at a 19% failure rate, about 30% versus 15%. Below-threshold motor GCS was associated with failure in two concordant studies (posterior median OR 5.99, 2.42-16.1; very low certainty). The pre-specified comparison between families could not be validly estimated from published data. An absent or weak cough at extubation is the best-supported single bedside predictor of failure after acute brain injury and should be assessed with secretions, swallowing and consciousness. Fewer than one in ten eligible studies are poolable, mainly for remediable reporting reasons; a minimum reporting set is proposed. PROSPERO CRD420261442541 (submitted 6 July 2026; registered 2 September 2026). Protocol v2.3 was prepared before the searches; the PROSPERO amendment and all deviations are listed in Supplementary Table S1. PRISMA 2020 [1].

papers.abstract: Prophylactic norepinephrine infusion has gained increasing attention to prevent intraoperative hypotension during major non-cardiac surgery, but its effect on haemodynamic stability, tissue perfusion, fluid administration, and postoperative outcomes remains uncertain. PubMed, Embase, and Cochrane CENTRAL were searched through May 9, 2026 for randomised trials comparing prophylactic norepinephrine with standard reactive management. Outcomes included change in serum lactate, haemodynamic measures, fluid administration, and postoperative outcomes, including complications and mortality. Risk of bias and certainty of evidence were assessed using Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 (RoB 2) and the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) approach, respectively. Sensitivity analyses and trial sequential analysis (TSA) were performed. Eleven trials (1688 patients) were included. Prophylactic norepinephrine was associated with a lower rise in lactate (mean difference (MD) -0.13 mmol/L, 95% CI -0.25 to -0.01; P = 0.03; I²=67.2%), higher post-induction mean arterial pressure (MD 10.79 mmHg, 95% CI 5.53 to 16.04; P < 0.01; I²=95.3%), higher postoperative mean arterial pressure (MD 2.78 mmHg, 95% CI 0.63 to 4.92; P = 0.01; I²=69.8%). Prophylactic norepinephrine use was associated with lower crystalloid administration (MD-548.22 mL, 95% CI -1087.16 to -9.28, P = 0.05, I²=99%) although substantial heterogeneity and protocol-driven differences limit interpretation. Exploratory analyses suggested lower incidences of myocardial infarction (RR 0.25, 95% CI 0.06-0.98), pneumonia (RR 0.58, 95% CI 0.36-0.95), and 30 day-surgical site infection (RR 0.63, 95% CI 0.41-0.97). No statistically significant differences were demonstrated for acute kidney injury, atelectasis, length of stay, or mortality. Certainty of evidence was low for most outcomes. TSA indicated insufficient evidence to establish a definitive treatment effect. Prophylactic norepinephrine was associated with a statistically significant but small reduction in intraoperative lactate rise, higher post-induction and post-operative mean arterial pressures. Postoperative complication findings remain exploratory and require confirmation in adequately powered randomised trials. PROSPERO (CRD420261345140).

papers.abstract: Regional analgesia is recommended for rib fractures, but utilization remains low. The extent to which hospital-level factors drive utilization and influence patient outcomes is unclear. This study's objective was to evaluate associations between hospital characteristics and regional analgesia receipt and outcomes. Retrospective cohort study using the Nationwide Inpatient Sample (NIS) of adult hospitalizations (>18 years) between January 1, 2016, and December 31, 2022 with rib fractures. Exposures included hospital bed-size, ownership, teaching status and geographic region. Primary outcome was regional analgesia receipt. Secondary outcomes included in-hospital mortality and tracheostomy. 250,630 hospitalizations met inclusion criteria, of which 7,179 (2.9%) received regional analgesia. After adjustment, 23.9% of variation in utilization was attributable to between-hospital differences. Greater utilization was associated with large hospital bed-size (odds ratio [OR] 2.08; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.80-2.39), urban teaching-status (OR 1.39; 95% CI, 1.19-1.62), higher income-quartile (OR 1.21; 95% CI, 1.10-1.33), and private insurance (OR 1.24; 95% CI, 1.14-1.35). Lower odds were observed in private nonprofit (OR 0.75; 95% CI, 0.65-0.86) and for-profit hospitals (OR 0.42; 95% CI, 0.34-0.53) compared with government hospitals. Regional analgesia utilization varied geographically, with the highest utilization in New England. Private insurance, White race, highest income quartile, government ownership and urban teaching status were also associated with earlier receipt of regional anesthesia. Disparities by insurance and hospital characteristics either persisted or widened from 2016 to 2022.Regional analgesia was associated with lower mortality (OR, 0.52; 95% CI, 0.42-0.64) and tracheostomy (OR, 0.48; 95% CI, 0.36-0.63) in multivariable analysis. In instrumental variable analysis with leave-one-out hospital-year regional analgesia rate as the instrument, these associations were attenuated. Regional analgesia remains infrequently utilized for rib fractures, with marked variation across hospitals. Access and outcomes appear to depend substantially on where patients receive care. Understanding the institutional and provider-level factors underlying this variation represents an important target for future quality-improvement and implementation efforts.

papers.abstract: Renal replacement therapy (RRT) is a life-saving intervention for acute kidney injury in the intensive care unit (ICU). The decision to initiate RRT remains highly complex and subjective. Accurate and timely predictions for the need of RRT initiation are crucial components of personalized care. Using time series patient data (vital signs, laboratory findings, medications, ventilator settings, intake/output, risk scores), we aimed to develop machine learning (ML) models for predicting future initiation of RRT. Using data from the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care (MIMIC)-III, MIMIC-IV, and Electronic ICU Collaborative Research Database (eICU), we trained and internally validated models using dataset-specific training, validation, and test splits. We externally validated model performance using held-out eICU hospitals excluded from model development and a temporally distinct cohort of ICU patients admitted during the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic period (2020-2022). Models were developed for: (1) screening patients for prediction of the need for RRT after their first 12 hours in the ICU; and (2) real-time dynamic prediction of the likelihood of documented RRT initiation within the next 24 hours. Here, we summarize the results of the ML model aimed at screening patients for early prediction of RRT. In internal validation, the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) was 0.90 (95% confidence interval [CI], 0.886-0.906) and the area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC) was 0.53 (95% CI, 0.496-0.564) in MIMIC-III. Results were similar in MIMIC-IV and eICU. External validation on ICU patients admitted during the coronavirus disease (COVID) period yielded an AUROC of 0.90 (95% CI, 0.894-0.913) and an AUPRC of 0.57 (95% CI, 0.534-0.602). Additional hospital-level external validation across eight individual eICU hospitals showed AUROCs ranging from 0.86 to 0.91 and AUPRCs ranging from 0.35 to 0.52. Accuracy ranged from 0.78 to 0.84 across validation experiments. By accurately identifying patients at high risk for RRT initiation, the early prediction ML model could serve as a triage tool to prompt closer nephrology evaluation or optimization of fluid and hemodynamic management before overt renal failure develops.

papers.abstract: The hyperinflammatory phenotype of acute respiratory failure (ARF) identifies patients with high mortality, but its underlying pathophysiology remains incompletely understood. Mitochondrial dysfunction may contribute to inflammation, oxidative stress, and cell injury in critical illness. We investigated whether plasma mitochondrial-associated proteins characterize the hyperinflammatory phenotype and whether they contribute to its association with mortality. We analyzed 285 emergency department patients with ARF and suspected or confirmed COVID-19. Inflammatory phenotypes were derived by latent class analysis using nine biomarkers and clinical indicators. A mitochondrial-protein score was calculated from 59 MitoCarta3.0-matched proteins, and mitochondrial clusters were derived by principal component analysis and k-means clustering. The primary outcome was 28-day mortality. Latent class analysis identified 185 hypoinflammatory (65%) and 100 hyperinflammatory (35%) patients, with a significant difference in 28-day mortality (14/185, 7.6% vs. 31/100, 31.0%; p < 0.001). The mitochondrial-protein score increased with the probability of hyperinflammation (ρ=0.46, p < 0.001). Forty-three of 59 mitochondrial-associated proteins were more abundant in the hyperinflammatory phenotype, with prominent differences in apoptosis regulation, oxidative stress, and oxidative phosphorylation proteins. In a mutually adjusted model, the hyperinflammatory phenotype remained associated with mortality (odds ratio [OR]=6.40, 95%CI:3.08-13.95; p < 0.001), whereas the mitochondrial-protein score was not (OR=0.83 per SD, 95%CI:0.58-1.17; p = 0.30). Mitochondrial clusters yielded consistent findings. The hyperinflammatory phenotype of ARF is characterized by increased plasma mitochondrial-associated proteins, linking inflammation with mitochondrial biology and cellular injury. This mitochondrial signature did not account for mortality independently of inflammatory phenotype, suggesting that it represents a biological component of the hyperinflammatory state.

papers.abstract: To determine the overall postoperative outcome and success, it is important to assess the occurrence of postoperative complications as well as patients' perception of their health outcomes. The aim of this study was to evaluate the association between self-reported quality of recovery and postoperative complications. This secondary analysis included data from three prospective observational studies evaluating quality of recovery in patients undergoing elective non-cardiac surgery. Self-reported quality of recovery was assessed using the Quality of Recovery-15 questionnaire (QoR-15), which was completed by patients preoperatively and on the first postoperative day. Postoperative complications were recorded between surgery and hospital discharge according to the Clavien-Dindo classification (CDC) of surgical complications. Binary logistic regression models were used to assess the association between self-reported quality of recovery and postoperative complications. A total of 1,151 patients were included in this secondary analysis. Of these, 361 (31.4%) experienced postoperative complications. The median difference between preoperative and postoperative QoR-15 sum scores was higher in patients with postoperative complications compared to patients without complications (34 [IQR: 15-51] vs. 22 [IQR: 7-41]; p < 0.001). We found a relevant association between a greater decline in QoR-15 scores from preoperative to first postoperative day and postoperative complications after adjusting for potential confounders (OR 1.18 [95% CI: 1.14;1.23], p < 0.001). The association with no or minor complications was stronger in heterogeneous populations with various types of surgical procedures than in patients with radical prostatectomy. Early self-reported quality of recovery is associated with the occurrence of postoperative complications after elective non-cardiac surgery. Whether this association may aid in identifying patients at risk of developing postoperative complications warrants further investigation.

papers.abstract: The choice of vasopressor during Caesarean delivery to prevent maternal hypotension remains debated. This study aimed to determine the concentration-dependent effects of vasopressors on pregnant myometrium, with and without oxytocin. In this prospective ex vivo study, myometrial samples were obtained from full-term pregnant women during elective Caesarean delivery. Myometrial contractility to vasopressors was recorded in the absence/presence of oxytocin compared with controls. Concentration-response testing was done with ephedrine, phenylephrine, and norepinephrine. The primary outcome was the motility index (amplitude×frequency). Isolated primary myometrial cells were also used for calcium mobilisation assays. Myometrial samples were obtained from 32 females. The mean motility index increased with ephedrine (+39.9%; 95% CI 20.6-62.5; P<0.001) and phenylephrine (+36.2%; 95% CI 19.3-55.4; P<0.001), but norepinephrine had no effect (+12.0%; 95% CI -0.7 to 26.1; P=0.066) compared with control. Similar changes in motility index were observed in the presence of oxytocin. Calcium mobilisation recordings on primary myometrial cells supported the contractility findings, with increases in intracellular calcium ions after ephedrine and phenylephrine, but not with norepinephrine compared with control. Ephedrine and phenylephrine increased ex vivo human myometrial contractility, both independently and in combination with oxytocin, consistent with improving uterine tone during Caesarean delivery. Norepinephrine does not affect myometrial contractility, suggesting that it is safe to use before delivery.

papers.abstract: Robotic-assisted gynaecological surgery commonly requires prolonged pneumoperitoneum and steep Trendelenburg positioning, which promote perioperative atelectasis and may increase complication risk. We aimed to investigate the effect of low pneumoperitoneum pressure (LPP) on atelectasis following robotic-assisted gynaecological surgery. We conducted a prospective, surgeon- and assessor-blind, randomised controlled trial in women undergoing elective robot-assisted laparoscopic gynaecological surgery. Participants were randomly allocated to the LPP (12 mmHg) or standard pneumoperitoneum pressure (SPP: 15 mmHg) group. Primary outcomes were modified lung ultrasound (mLUS) scores assessed after surgery and 30 min post-extubation. Secondary outcomes included incidence of atelectasis, percentage of desaturation in the post-anaesthesia care unit (PACU), lengths of PACU and hospital stay, surgeon satisfaction with the operative visual field, numeric rating scale pain score and modified clinical pulmonary infection score on postoperative day 1, and postoperative pulmonary complications 7 days postoperatively. Sixty patients were enrolled (30 per group). The mLUSs were significantly lower in the LPP group versus the SPP group postoperatively (P < 0.001) and 30 min post-extubation (P < 0.001), particularly in the posterolateral lung region (P < 0.001). Compared with the SPP group, the LPP group experienced a 1.59-fold reduction in the risk of postoperative atelectasis 30 min post-extubation in the PACU (P = 0.004). Other secondary outcomes showed no significant intergroup differences. A low pneumoperitoneum pressure during robotic-assisted gynaecological surgery reduced perioperative modified lung ultrasound scores and the incidence of early postoperative atelectasis. However, this imaging difference was not accompanied by significant improvements in oxygenation. Further studies powered for clinical pulmonary outcomes are needed. papers.abstract: This study evaluated efficacy and safety of intraoperative individualized stepwise positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP) titration guided by lung ultrasound (LUS) in reducing pulmonary atelectasis and complications in patients undergoing robotic-assisted radical prostatectomy or cystectomy (RARPC). This randomized trial included 88 patients undergoing elective RARPC. Patients were assigned to either standard ventilation (PEEP 4 cmH₂O; group C) or LUS-guided stepwise PEEP titration up to 12 cmH₂O (group R). Patients, outcome assessors, and the data analyst were blinded. The primary outcome was analyzed using a linear mixed-effects model, estimating the between-group difference in LUS score at 2 h after surgery. Group R showed significantly lower total LUS scores at 2 h after surgery (adjusted difference: -1.68, 95%CI: -2.89 to -0.47; p = 0.007) compared to group C. Likewise, significantly lower LUS scores were observed in Group R from the end of surgery onward. PEEP titration progressively reduced post-pneumoperitoneum atelectasis rates from 50% to 9.1%, at a highest PEEP level of 12 cmH₂O. Dynamic lung compliance in group R was significantly greater at Top compared with the control group (58.93 ± 3.48 vs. 49.91 ± 5.74 mL/cmH₂O; p < 0.001). Heart rate, mean arterial pressure, oxygen saturation, and end-tidal CO₂ were comparable at all time points. Both groups were comparable for intraoperative hypotension and bradycardia. Intraoperative LUS-guided individualized PEEP optimization significantly reduced the incidence of postoperative atelectasis and improved dynamic lung compliance without compromising hemodynamic stability in patients undergoing RARPC. Lung ultrasound offers a practical, effective, and non-invasive bedside tool for optimizing ventilation in high-risk surgical settings. This study was registered in ClinicalTrials.gov in March 2024 (ID: NCT06307704). The trial protocol is available through the ClinicalTrials.gov registry at https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06307704 .

papers.abstract: Perioperative ischemia-reperfusion injury (IRI) remains a significant cause of postoperative organ dysfunction and mortality after cardiac, vascular, transplant, and high-risk noncardiac surgery. Despite advances in anesthetic and surgical techniques, practical strategies to prevent IRI are limited. Growing evidence indicates that purinergic signaling, mediated by extracellular ATP, ADP, adenosine, and their receptors, centrally regulates inflammation, microvascular function, and tissue recovery during perioperative ischemia and reperfusion. This narrative review synthesizes preclinical, translational, and clinical evidence on purinergic mechanisms in perioperative IRI across major organ systems, including the heart, lungs, kidneys, liver, intestines, and brain, emphasizing pharmacological strategies and anesthetic interactions relevant to intraoperative and early postoperative management. During ischemia and early reperfusion, extracellular ATP released from injured cells activates P2 receptors, promoting inflammasome activation, endothelial dysfunction, and microcirculatory injury. Subsequent hydrolysis of ATP by ectonucleotidases CD39 and CD73 generates adenosine, which activates P1 receptors (Adora1, Adora2a, Adora2b, and Adora3) to suppress inflammation, improve perfusion, and enhance tissue protection. Hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF)-dependent upregulation of CD73 and A2B transcriptionally amplifies this ATP-to-adenosine transition, and miRNAs post-transcriptionally modulate it. Pharmacological approaches targeting these pathways represent promising strategies for perioperative organ protection, whereas clinical evidence supporting anesthetic regimen selection for purinergic modulation remains insufficient. The efficacy of conditioning strategies, including ischemic preconditioning and remote ischemic preconditioning (RIPC), remains controversial, with negative large-scale trials highlighting the translational gap between preclinical models and multimorbid surgical patients. Purinergic signaling provides a unifying mechanistic framework for perioperative ischemia-reperfusion injury and represents a promising target for pharmacological organ protection. Prioritize pharmacological strategies that enhance adenosine generation, activate protective adenosine receptors, or inhibit ATP-P2X7-driven inflammation in perioperative clinical trials. Understanding how comorbidities and concomitant medications modulate purinergic pathways is essential for successful clinical translation.

papers.abstract: Controversy remains regarding the effect of inspired oxygen fraction (FIO2) on postoperative lung aeration. We sought to evaluate whether lowering FIO2 solely during emergence from anesthesia reduces immediate postoperative loss of lung aeration, assessed by lung ultrasonography. In this double-blind multicentre randomized controlled trial, we allocated 102 patients undergoing laparoscopic gastrectomy to either a low- or high-FIO2 group (FIO2 = 0.5 vs 0.8 during emergence, respectively). The primary outcome was the lung ultrasonography score (LUS) measured in the postanesthesia care unit (PACU). Secondary outcomes were the Oxygen Reserve Index™ (ORi™) after extubation, atelectasis on chest radiography taken on postoperative day (POD) 2, and oxygen desaturation events in the PACU and within the first 48 postoperative hr. The median [interquartile range (IQR)] LUS did not significantly differ between the two groups (low-FIO2 group, 3 [2-5] vs high-FIO2 group, 3 [2-6]; P = 0.48). The median [IQR] ORi values after extubation were 0.42 [0.10-0.74] and 0.52 [0.30-0.83] in the low- and high-FIO2 groups, respectively (adjusted P = 0.36). The incidence of atelectasis on chest radiography on POD 2 (low-FIO2 group, 57% vs high-FIO2 group, 49%; P = 0.43; adjusted P > 0.99) and other pulmonary complication rates were not different between the groups. Lowering the FIO2 from 0.8 to 0.5 during the anesthesia emergence period alone did not reduce immediate postoperative LUS after laparoscopic gastrectomy. Routine reduction of the FIO2 < 0.8 during emergence solely for the purpose of preserving postoperative lung aeration may have limited clinical value in a relatively low-risk patient population. papers.abstract: Intraoperative electroencephalography (EEG) allows real-time assessment of the anesthetic state of the brain and offers a means of titrating anesthetic delivery in children. Randomized trials have shown that EEG-guided titration reduces anesthetic exposure, shortens emergence and recovery, and lowers the incidence of emergence delirium, yet routine use outside research settings has remained largely confined to enthusiastic clinicians and clinical trials. To describe the adoption of routine intraoperative raw EEG monitoring over time at a quaternary pediatric hospital, to characterize practice variation among anesthesia providers, and to identify patient and procedural factors associated with EEG use. We conducted a retrospective single-center study of anesthetic records in the electronic health record from 17 October 2024, when automated EEG capture began, to 30 June 2026, following departmental implementation of routine raw EEG monitoring. Providers were categorized by EEG use as high (> 40% of cases), moderate (20%-40%) or low (< 20%). Trend, provider-level, and procedural associations with EEG use were examined using segmented regression, mixed-effects logistic regression, and clustered logistic regression. Of 26 168 analyzed cases, 21.7% (5674) involved intraoperative EEG monitoring, provided by 59 staff anesthesiologists, 9 senior fellows, 24 fellows, and 102 residents. EEG use rose from 17.8% of cases in October 2024 to 28.4% in June 2026. Use varied widely among staff anesthesiologists (median 18.1%, IQR 12.3%-31.3%; range 0.9%-79.5%); 59.3% (35/59) were low users, and 18.6% (11/59) were high users, with the five highest users accounting for 27.0% of all EEG-monitored cases managed by staff. Case mix explained only a small proportion of this variation (pseudo R2 = 0.064). EEG-monitored cases were more often longer, involved neuromuscular blockade, TIVA maintenance, cardiac surgery, and trainee presence. Adoption of routine raw EEG monitoring increased steadily but nonlinearly following implementation. Variation in use among providers was only weakly explained by case mix, indicating that individual practice patterns, more than patient or procedural characteristics, drove uptake. Efforts to broaden EEG monitoring may benefit from targeting low-use providers and during fellowship training.
